# Generate

Every generator is a method on the bound engine:

```ts
engine.collectVars(); // ConfigDef[] across every scope
engine.requiredEnvVars('server'); // required var names for a scope

engine.writeEnvFile({ output: '.env.example' });
engine.writeEnvTypes({ outputDir: 'types' });
engine.writeConfigTypes({ outputDir: 'types' });
engine.writeJsonSchema({ output: 'config.schema.json' });
engine.writeMarkdown({ outDir: 'docs/reference/configuration' });

engine.generateCliOptions({ output: 'cli-options.json' });
engine.buildConfigJson(); // the config metadata document
```

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config-generator/generated-outputs.md
---
# Generated outputs

Every generator writes from the same Zod schema. The engine's own config model
is the living example: its types are committed at
[packages/shared/src/config-types.ts](https://github.com/deltabox-studio/toolchain/blob/main/packages/shared/src/config-types.ts).

## Config types — `generateConfigTypes()` / `writeConfigTypes()`

Named `interface`s (and `type` aliases for enums/unions) with jsdoc taken from
`.describe()`. Unions and refs stay named, so nested objects are referenced
rather than inlined:

```ts
// engine.generateConfigTypes() -> { server: "...", cli: "..." }
engine.writeConfigTypes({ outputDir: 'types' }); // types/server.ts, types/cli.ts
```

```ts
// types/server.ts
export interface ServerConfig {
    /** Bind host. */
    host?: string;
    port?: number;
    auth?: { password?: string; enabled?: boolean };
}
```

An object schema that also accepts arbitrary keys (Zod `.catchall(...)` /
`.passthrough()`, ie. `additionalProperties` in the JSON Schema) generates an
open interface with an index signature, so the extra keys stay typed as
`unknown` instead of being rejected:

```ts
export interface ServerConfig {
    /** Bind host. */
    host?: string;
    [key: string]: unknown;
}
```

## Markdown — `writeMarkdown()`

One reference page per scope plus an index listing the required/core env vars:

```ts
engine.writeMarkdown({ outDir: 'docs/reference/configuration' });
// docs/reference/configuration/server.md, .../index.md
```

See a real full example at [config/reference.md](../../config/reference.md).

## Env — `renderEnvFile()` / `writeEnvFile()`

A `.env.example`; secrets are emitted commented out so operators fill them in:

```sh
engine.writeEnvFile({ output: '.env.example' });

# ---- SERVER ----
MYAPP_HOST=localhost
# MYAPP_AUTH_PASSWORD=
```

## JSON Schema — `generateJsonSchema()` / `writeJsonSchema()`

The resolved untyped JSON Schema for every scope, for editor autocomplete:

```ts
await engine.writeJsonSchema({ output: 'config.schema.json' });
```

## Formatting — `formatGenerated()`

Generated text is formatted **at generation time**, so a written file is already
formatted instead of relying on a separate `yarn format` pass. `formatGenerated`
runs source through Oxfmt, preferring the project-local `vite-plus/fmt` (Oxfmt
ships with Vite+), then `oxfmt`, and returns the input untouched when no formatter
is resolvable, so generation never fails on a missing formatter.

```ts
import { formatGenerated, GENERATED_FORMAT_OPTIONS } from '@deltabox/toolchain/config';

const source = 'export const config={a:1}';
const formatted = await formatGenerated(source, {
    fileName: 'config.ts', // infers the language (default `generated.ts`)
    options: { printWidth: 100 }, // merged over GENERATED_FORMAT_OPTIONS
});
```

`GENERATED_FORMAT_OPTIONS` is the baseline Oxfmt config matching the toolchain's
own `vite.config.ts` (4-space indent, single quotes, `trailingComma: 'es5'`,
`jsdoc: true`, ...). Pass `options.fileName` to format JSON, markdown or another
language, and `options.options` to override any single option.

For a full, real example of the generated config types, see
`packages/shared/src/config-types.ts`.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/hooks.md
---
# Hooks

`.ts`/`.js` configs can declare lifecycle hooks (JSON cannot):

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        hooks: {
            afterLoad: ({ tokens }) => console.log(tokens),
            beforeSync: ctx => ctx.log('syncing…'),
            afterTask: ({ task, files }) => console.log(task.name, files?.length),
            afterSync: ({ result }) => console.log(result.written.length),
            onChange: ({ path }) => console.log('changed', path),
        },
    },
});
```

Return values are awaited.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config-generator/load-the-config.md
---
# Load the config at runtime

Generation is only half of it. The same schema backs a small, dependency-free
**loader**. `parseEnvTree` folds `PREFIX_*` variables into a nested tree
(splitting the remainder on `_`), and the typed accessors read dotted paths out
of it:

```ts
import {
    envBool,
    envInt,
    envList,
    envMap,
    envString,
    parseEnvTree,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain/config';
import { applyOverrides } from '@deltabox/toolchain/shared';

// MYAPP_HOST, MYAPP_PORT, MYAPP_LOG_PRETTY, ... -> a nested tree
const tree = parseEnvTree(process.env, 'MYAPP_');

const config = {
    host: envString(tree, 'host', '0.0.0.0'),
    port: envInt(tree, 'port', 3000),
    pretty: envBool(tree, 'log.pretty', true),
    corsOrigins: envList(tree, 'cors.origin', []),
    headers: envMap(tree, 'response.headers.map'), // `Key=value,...` -> record
};
```

| Helper                       | Reads                                                |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `envString(tree, path, fb?)` | string (unset/empty -> fallback)                     |
| `envInt` / `envBool`         | number / boolean (`true/1/yes/on`, `false/0/no/off`) |
| `envList`                    | comma-separated list                                 |
| `envMap`                     | `Key=value,...` into a lowercase-keyed record        |
| `readEnvPath(tree, path)`    | the raw value at a dotted path                       |

Layer typed overrides on top of the env values (a config file, then CLI flags)
with `applyOverrides`, then validate the result through the scope schema so it is
guaranteed to match the generated types:

```ts
import { compileZodSchema } from '@deltabox/toolchain/config';

const schemaCompiler = compileZodSchema(serverConfig);

export function loadConfig(env = process.env, file = {}, cli = {}) {
    const tree = parseEnvTree(env, 'MYAPP_');
    const fromEnv = {
        base: {
            host: envString(tree, 'host', '0.0.0.0'),
            port: envInt(tree, 'port', 3000),
        },
        auth: {
            password: envString(tree, 'auth.password', ''),
            tokenTtl: envInt(tree, 'auth.token.ttl', 3600),
        },
    };
    return schemaCompiler.parse(applyOverrides(fromEnv, file, cli));
}
```

A resolver like this is the runtime counterpart of the generators — same schema,
same defaults, one typed object out.

> The dotted path is the env name with the prefix removed and `_` folded to `.`,
> so `MYAPP_AUTH_TOKEN_TTL` reads as `auth.token.ttl`. When a field name differs
> from its env-derived path, map it explicitly in the resolver (as above).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/api/logging.md
---
# Logging

Every toolchain message goes through one level-aware logger, rendered with
[`@clack/prompts`](https://bombshell.dev/clack) (level symbols + guide). Use it
instead of `console.log` so output stays consistent and respects the config and
the CLI flags.

| Export / member                                   | Description                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `logger`                                          | The active singleton: `raw`, `debug`, `info`, `success`, `warn`, `error`, `level`, `colors`. |
| `createLogger(options)`                           | Create an independent logger (`level`, `color`, `name`).                                     |
| `setLogConfig(section)`                           | Apply the `logger` section from the loaded config.                                           |
| `setLogOverrides(options)`                        | Apply CLI overrides (win over the config). `configureLogger` is an alias.                    |
| `getLogOverrides()` / `getLogger()`               | Read the current overrides / the active instance.                                            |
| `LOG_LEVELS` / `isLogLevel` / `normalizeLogLevel` | The valid levels, most verbose first (`debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, `silent`).           |

```ts
import { createLogger, logger, setLogConfig, setLogOverrides } from '@deltabox/toolchain/shared';

setLogConfig({ level: 'debug', color: false, name: 'dbx' }); // from dbx.config.*
setLogOverrides({ level: 'warn' }); // from --log-level

logger.info('human message');
logger.success('done');
logger.error('failed');
logger.raw(JSON.stringify(payload)); // machine output: no prefix, no colour
```

Use `raw` for machine output (`--json`): it is never prefixed or decorated.
`logger.warn`/`error` write to stderr; `debug`/`info`/`success`/`raw` to stdout.
Messages that start with whitespace (indented continuations) are never prefixed.

This mirrors the [`logger` config section](/guide/config/logging) and the
`--log-level <level>` / `--no-color` [CLI flags](/guide/cli#global-flags), which
call `setLogConfig` / `setLogOverrides` under the hood.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/logging.md
---
# Logging

Every toolchain message goes through one logger. Configure it in the config:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        logger: { level: 'debug', color: false, name: 'dbx' },
    },
});
```

| Option     | Values                                             | Default |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `level`    | `debug` | `info` | `warn` | `error` | `silent` | `info`  |
| `color`    | `true` | `false`                                  | `true`  |
| `name`     | prefix for non-indented lines                      | `dbx`   |
| `suppress` | id, message substring or `/regex/` (single/array)  | none    |

`suppress` silences matching warnings/errors. A string matches an emitted id
exactly or a message substring; a `/pattern/flags` string is treated as a regex.
Ids are rendered in uppercase in the output (eg. `[FMT_CONFLICT]`), but match
the lowercase id when suppressing. It accepts one value or an array:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
toolchain: {
    logger: {
        suppress: ['fmt.conflict', 'deprecated option', '/^Could not .* globally/'],
    },
}
```

Colour is **on by default** (the toolchain forces it rather than relying on TTY
autodetection); `--no-color` or `logger: { color: false }` turn it off. Human
output is rendered with [`@clack/prompts`](https://bombshell.dev/clack) — level
symbols (`•` info, `◆` success, `▲` warn, `■` error) and a guide.

On the CLI, `--log-level <level>` and `--no-color` override the config (see the
[CLI reference](/guide/cli)). Machine output (`--json`) is written unprefixed
through the same logger.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/nested-configs.md
---
# Nested configs

A `dbx.config.*` in a **non-root** folder (a workspace, an app, a nested
project) is merged over the nearest ancestor `dbx.config.*` found while walking
up to the repository root (the walk stops at the `.git` boundary, so it never
picks up a config from outside the repo).

The merge is recursive:

* **Objects** are merged key by key, so a child keeps every option it does not
  mention.
* **Leaves** — booleans, strings, numbers and **arrays** — in the child
  **replace** the root's value (arrays are not concatenated).
* **Repository-scoped sections are not inherited**: `ci` and the top-level
  `changelog`, `tsconfig`, `vite.test` and `vite.run`. A workflow,
  workspace tsconfig tree, test config or task list describes the repository or
  one workspace, so a child starts without the parent's values for them. In
  particular, the root `tsconfig` task already expands every workspace
  `tsconfig.json`; inheriting it into each workspace would only re-scan that
  subtree.

Everything else is shared unless the child overrides it — `vite.fmt`,
`vite.lint`, `vite.plugins`, `logger`, `biome`, `templates`, `registry`, and so
on — so lint/format settings are cohesive across a monorepo by default.

```ts [<root>/dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        logger: { level: 'debug', color: false },
        vite: {
            fmt: { printWidth: 100, singleQuote: true },
        },
    },
});

// <root>/packages/web/dbx.config.ts — inherits `vite.fmt`, tweaks `logger`
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        logger: { level: 'warn' }, // leaf overrides the root's level
        vite: {
            run: { tasks: { build: { command: 'tsdown' } } }, // not inherited
        },
    },
});
```

The workspace above ends up with `logger: { level: 'warn', color: false }` and
the root's `vite.fmt` settings. Its `vite.run` holds only the `build` task it
declares — the root's tasks are not merged in.

> **Arrays replace, so repeat what you need.** If a workspace sets
> `vite.fmt.ignorePatterns`, that array replaces the root's list (it is not
> appended). Either keep the root patterns in the workspace array, or put the
> shared pattern on the root config — for example `**/vite.config.ts` there
> covers every workspace's generated shim.

> **`project` is inherited except its identity fields.** `name`, `scope`,
> `description` and `type` are per-project, so a non-root config keeps its own (or
> falls back to its `package.json`) and is still detected from its own files — a
> root `project` never renames a workspace. The shared fields (`author`,
> `license`, `homepage`, `repo`, `packageManager`, ...) flow down so their
> `package.json` values and replacement tokens stay shared.
> `project: { inherit: false }` disables project inheritance entirely. `hooks`
> are not inherited either — a parent's hooks are code and do not run for a
> nested project's sync.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/opt-in-by-presence.md
---
# Opt-in by presence

Every section under `toolchain` is **opt-in by presence**: the toolchain only
touches an area you actually ask for.

* Omit a section — that area is left completely alone.
* `section: true` — enable it with defaults (when the section has defaults).
* `section: false` — explicitly disable it.
* `section: { ...options }` — enable and configure it.

This applies to nested sections too. `ci` is opt-in, and every workflow inside it
(`ci.ci`, `ci.release`, `ci.issues`, `ci.changelog`, `ci.sync`) is opt-in as
well: omit a workflow (or set it to `false`) and the toolchain will not generate
or manage its file. Setting `ci: false` or `ci: { enabled: false }` disables the
whole section, including every nested workflow and the changelog pipeline.

The same rule backs `ci.changelog`: it is only managed when you declare it, and
`ci.changelog: false` (or `enabled: false`) disables both its workflow and the
changelog pipeline.

Helpers `sectionEnabled(section)` and `sectionConfig(section)` implement this and
are exported for programmatic use.

The top-level `changelog` section configures the manual pipeline for `dbx
changelog`/the API. It does not enable CI by itself; `ci.changelog` inherits its
options when they are not overridden. See
[Manual `toolchain.changelog`](/guide/changelog/#manual-toolchainchangelog).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/api/package-reference.md
---
# Package reference

## `@deltabox/toolchain/shared`

The base layer: the config model, logging, process/string/object utilities and
the template engine.

| Export                                                                        | Description                                                                              |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `defineConfig(config)`                                                        | Identity helper for a typed `dbx.config.*` (object, promise, or sync/async callback).    |
| `sectionEnabled(section)` / `sectionConfig(section)`                          | Opt-in-by-presence helpers for a config section.                                         |
| `resolveTokens(config)`                                                       | Flatten a config into `{{ token }}` replacements.                                        |
| `CONFIG_FILE_NAMES`                                                           | The config file names the loader probes, in priority order.                              |
| `repoSlugFromUrl(url)`                                                        | Derive an `owner/name` slug from a repository URL.                                       |
| `findOwnCliEntry(cwd?)` / `localToolchainVersion(cwd?)` / `TOOLCHAIN_PACKAGE` | Locate a project's own toolchain bin + pinned version (prefer them over a global `dbx`). |
| `createLogger(options)` / `logger`                                            | The shared logger (see [Logging](/guide/api/logging)).                                   |
| `WARNING_MAP` / `ERROR_MAP` / `warningMessage(id, values?)`                   | Central messages keyed by stable logger/suppression ids.                                 |
| `spawnCross(cmd, args, options)` / `run(cmd, args, options)`                  | Cross-platform, shell-free spawning; `timeoutMs` kills the child tree.                   |
| `killProcessTree(child)`                                                      | Kill a child process and its descendants (Windows `taskkill /t`).                        |
| `readJsonFile` / `readJsonAt` / `toJson` / `writeJsonFile`                    | Small JSON file helpers.                                                                 |
| `mergeJsonAt(cwd, relative, patch)`                                           | Deep-merge a patch over an existing JSON file.                                           |
| `deepMerge` / `applyOverrides` / `isPlainObject` / `sort` / `mapValues`       | Object utilities (including layered typed overrides).                                    |
| `applyReplacements` / `applyReplacementsDeep` / `createReplacer`              | The `{{ token }}` template engine (also `tokenPattern`, `extractTokens`).                |
| `toYaml(value)`                                                               | A tiny YAML emitter for the GitHub Actions subset.                                       |

The config **types** and **schemas** also live here: `ToolchainConfig`, `DbxConfig`,
`SyncTask`, `SyncContext`, `ManagedFile`, `ToolchainCommand`, `ToolchainOption`,
`ToolchainProvider`, `ToolchainViteConfig` (Vite+'s config type), `Replacements`,
and the generated `config-types` / `config-schema` exports.

```ts
import { defineConfig, sectionEnabled, applyReplacements } from '@deltabox/toolchain/shared';

const text = applyReplacements('Hello {{name:world}}', { name: 'acme' });
```

## `@deltabox/toolchain/core`

Loads `dbx.config.*`, builds the project graph and runs the sync tasks.

| Export                                                        | Description                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |

# Programmatic API

```ts
import { loadToolchainConfig, runSync, defaultSyncTasks } from '@deltabox/toolchain';

const { config, tokens, projectType } = await loadToolchainConfig(process.cwd());
await runSync({ tasks: defaultSyncTasks(), cwd: process.cwd(), config, tokens, projectType });
```

Full section reference: [dbx.config](/config/reference).

# Providers

Provider passthrough commands (Vite+) follow the logger's colour setting. The
`providers` section can force provider colours on or off on its own:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        providers: { color: false },
    },
});
```

| Option  | Values            | Default        |
| ------- | ----------------- | -------------- |
| `color` | `true` | `false` | inherit logger |

`color: false` runs the wrapped binary with `NO_COLOR=1` and `FORCE_COLOR=0`, so
it emits plain output even on a colour terminal. The global CLI `--no-color`
flag turns provider colour off too. See [Providers](/guide/providers#colour).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config-generator/real-world-shape.md
---
# Real-world shape

Proxified binds three scopes under a `PROXIFIED_` prefix and reuses the engine
for every generator:

```ts
import { createConfigEngine } from '@deltabox/toolchain/config';

export const configEngine = createConfigEngine({
    schema: {
        server: serverConfig,
        frontend: frontendConfig,
        cli: cliConfig,
    },
    envPrefix: 'PROXIFIED_',
    baseGroup: 'base',
    root: monorepoRoot(),
    envPathOf: env => envPathOf(env),
});
```

The generators then run from a `config:generate-all` script (built on the
`configCommands({ engine })` helpers) to keep `.env.example`, the JSON Schema,
the markdown reference, the types and the CLI options in sync with the schemas.

These `config:*` commands belong to the consumer's own CLI, `dbx`
itself does not expose them.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/api/registering-commands.md
---
# Registering commands

Packages export framework-agnostic `ToolchainCommand[]` descriptors; wire them onto
a commander program with `registerToolchainCommands` (this is how the bundled
`dbx` binary, and a consumer's own CLI, are assembled):

```ts
import { Command } from 'commander';

import { registerToolchainCommands } from '@deltabox/toolchain/cli';
import { configCommands } from '@deltabox/toolchain/config';

const program = new Command();
registerToolchainCommands(program, configCommands({ engine }));
await program.parseAsync();
```

# Troubleshooting

## `No "exports" main defined in … conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits`

Seen from the Conventional Commits VS Code extension (`vivaxy.vscode-conventional-commits`),
usually alongside empty type/scope suggestions and a `The cwd is …` line:

```
commitlint: Error: No "exports" main defined in
  node_modules/conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits/package.json
```

This is a **known upstream commitlint bug** (commitlint#4864): the generated
config `extends: ['@commitlint/config-conventional']`, which sets
`parserPreset: 'conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits'`, and v10 of that
package is **ESM-only** (`exports` has no `require`/`default`), so the extension's
bundled (older) commitlint cannot `require.resolve` it. The config is read fine —
the *preset* fails to resolve, so the extension falls back to empty rules.

The husky hook and CI are unaffected when commitlint is recent enough to resolve
pure-ESM presets (commitlint ≥ 21.2.3). If your local commitlint is older, pin
the preset to the last CJS-compatible release:

```json [package.json]
{
    "resolutions": { "conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits": "9.3.1" }
}
```

(Use `overrides` instead of `resolutions` for npm.) Updating the extension to a
version bundling the fixed commitlint also resolves it.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/api/umbrella.md

# Umbrella (`@deltabox/toolchain`)

The root re-exports `@deltabox/toolchain-core` and `@deltabox/toolchain-shared`
**directly**, and exposes the remaining packages as **namespaces** plus the sync
runner:

```ts
import {
    // identity helper (typed config)
    defineConfig,
    // config + sync
    loadToolchainConfig,
    runSync,
    runWatch,
    defaultSyncTasks,
    // opt-in-by-presence helpers
    sectionEnabled,
    sectionConfig,
    resolveTokens,
    // logging
    logger,
    createLogger,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain';
// The other packages are namespaced:
import {
    biome,
    changelog,
    config,
    core,
    project,
    shared,
    tsconfig,
    tsdown,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain';
```

```ts
const { config, tokens, projectType } = await loadToolchainConfig(process.cwd());
await runSync({ tasks: defaultSyncTasks(), cwd: process.cwd(), config, tokens, projectType });
```

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/changelog/versioning.md
---
# Versioning

`ci.changelog.versioning` controls whether — and where — a changelog run writes
`version` fields into `package.json`. It accepts a boolean or an object, and
defaults to `true`.

```ts
ci: { changelog: { versioning: true } }                       // uniform, defaults
ci: { changelog: { versioning: false } }                      // never write versions
ci: { changelog: { versioning: { target: 'root-only' } } }
ci: { changelog: { versioning: { target: 'individual', workspaces: ['packages/*'] } } }
```

## `target`

| Target       | What it bumps                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `uniform`    | The root (when it has a `package.json`) **and every workspace** to one shared version. **Default.**                                                                          |
| `root-only`  | Only the root `package.json`. Workspaces are left untouched and get no changelog entry.                                                                                      |
| `individual` | The root tracks the overall bump; **each workspace is bumped on its own** from the commits touching its files, so versions can drift apart (like an "independent" monorepo). |

With `versioning: false` no `version` field is written at all — the changelog
entries are still generated (headed as `uniform` would), so you can keep
versioning in another tool (for example changesets).

## `workspaces`

An array of glob patterns selecting the workspaces to version, relative to the
repo root. It resolves in this order:

1. the `workspaces` patterns you pass, when you pass them;
2. otherwise the root `package.json` `workspaces` field, when present;
3. otherwise the root `package.json` alone (a single-package repo);
4. otherwise a warning is logged and nothing is versioned.

```ts
ci: {
    changelog: {
        versioning: {
            target: 'individual',
            workspaces: ['packages/*', '!packages/private-*'],
        },
    },
}
```

`individual` uses a `git log` path filter per workspace, so a workspace is only
bumped when the scanned commit range touched a file inside it — or a file in one
of the workspaces it depends on (see [Workspace changelogs](#workspace-changelogs)).
The root's version always follows the overall bump derived from every scanned
commit.

## How a run decides its versions

Each run:

1. reads the commits in the range (`--range`/`--processing-method`, default
   `HEAD`);
2. derives the semver bump (`feat` → minor, `fix`/other → patch, `!` or a
   `BREAKING CHANGE` footer → major);
3. plans the versions per `target` + `workspaces` (see above);
4. writes the plan's `package.json` versions and prepends the new entry to the
   root `CHANGELOG.md` and each versioned workspace's `CHANGELOG.md`.

Use `dbx changelog --dry-run` to preview the proposed root entry without touching
any file; the log line reports the active `target` (or `disabled`).

## Workspace changelogs

Each versioned workspace gets **its own `CHANGELOG.md`** (created if missing),
headed by the version the plan assigned it. A workspace's entry only lists its
**related commits**: those touching the workspace directory **or any workspace it
transitively depends on**, resolved from the project dependency graph
(`.dbx/toolchain/projects.json`, written by `dbx projects`). So a change in a
shared package shows up in the changelog of every package that consumes it, not
just in its own.

Without a graph (eg. `dbx projects` was never run), a workspace falls back to
filtering on its own directory only. A workspace with no related commits is
skipped (no empty entry, no file created).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config/vite.md
---
# Vite+

The whole Vite+ config lives in `toolchain.vite`. Every key is passed through
verbatim to Vite+, so `dbx.config.*` stays the only hand-authored root config:

```ts [dbx.config.ts]
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        vite: {
            test: { include: ['src/**/*.test.ts'], environment: 'node' },
            lint: { ignorePatterns: ['dist/**'] },
            fmt: { semi: true, singleQuote: true },
        },
    },
});
```

`dbx sync` writes a thin root `vite.config.ts` that resolves that config at load
time, so the generated file never duplicates (or drifts from) `dbx.config.*`:

```ts [vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig, type ViteUserConfig } from 'vite-plus';

// Generated by @deltabox/toolchain — edit the vite section in dbx.config and run `dbx sync`.
import { resolveVite } from '@deltabox/toolchain/vite';

export default defineConfig(resolveVite<ViteUserConfig>({ cwd: import.meta.dirname }));
```

The shim imports `defineConfig` from whichever Vite package the project installs
(`vite` or `vite-plus`, detected from `package.json`), so a plain `vite` project
gets `import { defineConfig, type UserConfig } from 'vite'` and
`resolveVite<UserConfig>(...)`.

`resolveVite(options?)` resolves the **same-directory** `dbx.config.*` (so a
nested `vite.config.ts` uses the nested config it sits next to), or the
`toolchain` you pass, then returns `toolchain.vite`. Pass `vite` inline to merge
overrides over the loaded section (`resolveVite({ vite: { ... } })`). It is
exported from `@deltabox/toolchain/vite` for programmatic use too.

The single toolchain opt-out is `config`. Set `vite: { config: false }` to leave
a hand-written `vite.config.ts` alone; set `config` to a string (relative to the
project, or absolute) to write the managed shim at a different path instead.
Everything else under `vite` is Vite+ config (plugins, `test`, `lint`, `fmt`,
`run.tasks`, ...), so `toolchain.vite` is the full Vite+ configuration. The section is typed as Vite+'s own config
(`ToolchainViteConfig` = Vite's `UserConfig` as augmented by Vite+), so the whole
Vite+ surface autocompletes in `dbx.config.ts`.

Add the shim to `vite.fmt.ignorePatterns` so Oxfmt leaves the generated file
alone - without it `vp fmt` would rewrite the shim and `dbx sync --check` would
report drift. In a monorepo put `**/vite.config.ts` on the root config: workspace
`fmt` settings are inherited, but a workspace's `ignorePatterns` array replaces
the root's list. `dbx migrate --from vite` adds it for you.

## Format and lint defaults

Opt in with `vite: { fmt: true }` / `vite: { lint: true }` to use the toolchain
defaults (`DEFAULT_FMT_RULES` / `DEFAULT_LINT_RULES`, exported from
`@deltabox/toolchain`). An options object is merged over those defaults, so
`fmt: { semi: false }` keeps the shared ignores and print width and only changes
`semi`. Shared ignore lists live in `DEFAULT_FMT_IGNORE_PATTERNS` /
`DEFAULT_LINT_IGNORE_PATTERNS`. `sortImports` is never included by default:
import ordering is project-specific, so opt in with your own groups.

## Oxc config files

Vite+ reads `fmt`/`lint` from `vite.config.ts`, but the Oxc VS Code extension
reads `.oxfmtrc.json` / `.oxlintrc.json`. When `vite.fmt` / `vite.lint` are
defined, `dbx sync` writes those files as managed files so the editor picks up
the same configuration. Only the root gets them by default; a nested
`dbx.config.*` gets its own pair only when it defines `vite.fmt` / `vite.lint`
itself (an inherited root config does not create per-workspace files).

To adopt an existing hand-written `vite.config.ts`, fold it in with the
migration (see [Migrations](/guide/migrations#vite-config)):

```sh
dbx migrate --from vite --write   # folds the object into toolchain.vite (+ the fmt ignore)
dbx sync                          # writes the managed vite.config.ts shim
```

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/changelog/writing-commit-messages.md
---
# Writing commit messages

The changelog is rendered from commit **subjects and bodies**, so what you commit
is what readers see. Watch out for characters that a **shell** re-interprets —
especially when a message is drafted by an **AI/LLM** and committed through
`git commit -m "…"`.

## Shell escaping

* **PowerShell** treats a backtick as its escape character, so `` `r `` / `` `n `` /
  `` `t `` / `` `b `` become CR / LF / TAB / backspace. A preceding `\` is left
  behind, so `` `resolveVite `` can land in the changelog as a stray `\`, a CR and
  `esolveVite`.
* **bash** runs an unquoted `` `…` `` as command substitution, and `$(…)` / `${…}`
  expand before `git` ever sees them.

The result is invisible control characters, stray `\` and dropped letters. The
toolchain strips the predictable artifacts
(`stripControlChars`/`sanitizeText`) but **cannot restore a character the shell
already consumed**.

## Authoring safely

* Prefer a **file over `-m`**: `git commit -F message.txt`, or a quoted heredoc
  (`git commit -F - <<'EOF' … EOF`) — nothing is re-interpreted. Avoid assembling
  multi-line messages inline in PowerShell.
* When an AI/LLM drafts the message, strip **typographic characters** before
  committing: curly quotes (`’ “ ”`), em/en dashes (`— –`), non-breaking spaces,
  zero-width characters and emoji all survive into the changelog and can break
  `commitlint` or the markdown.
* **Preview the entry**: `dbx changelog --dry-run` prints the proposed entry —
  check it for stray `\`, `\r`, `\b`, `\t` or mojibake before releasing.
